content: The mons pubis, also referred to as the mons veneris (Latin for mound of Venus) or simply the mons, is a soft, rounded mound of tissue located in women just above the genital region. This elevation is due to a layer of subcutaneous fat that lies beneath the skin, providing cushioning and protection to the underlying pubic bone. Anatomically, it is situated anterior to the symphysis pubis. The size of the mons pubis varies depending on an individual's overall body fat composition. Following puberty, it is typically covered with pubic hair. In humans, the mons pubis transitions into the labia majora (literally meaning major lips) on either side of a central groove, known as the cleft of Venus. This groove encompasses the clitoris, vaginal opening, and other structures of the vulva. The fatty tissue of the mons veneris is highly responsive to estrogen. During puberty, the influence of estrogen leads to the development of a distinct mound in this region. This growth causes the anterior portion of the labia majora to project outward and away from the pubic bone, aligning parallel to the ground when the individual is in a standing position.
